lead: Two phases of a pure substance coexist in equilibrium along one curve in the p-T plane, the saturation line. There their Gibbs functions are equal. Differentiating that equality along the line gives dp/dT in terms of latent heat and volume change: the Clapeyron equation. Its liquid-vapour form, the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, converts vapour-pressure data into latent heats, predicts boiling points, and explains regelation.
prereq: You need 4.3 for equal Gibbs functions at phase equilibrium and dg = v dp − s dT, and 4.4 for turning differentials into measurable slopes; saturation data come from Unit 5, Pure Substances.

sections.h3: Equal Gibbs functions fix the slope of the saturation line

blocks.text: Take a pure substance with two phases, say liquid and vapour, at pressure p and temperature T. Equilibrium means no reason to leave one phase for the other. From 4.3, this requires equal specific Gibbs functions: g₁ = g₂, with g in kJ/kg.

Move a small step along the saturation line: T rises by dT, p by dp, both phases stay in equilibrium. Each phase changes by dg = v dp − s dT, where v is specific volume (m³/kg) and s is specific entropy (kJ/kg·K). Equality must persist, so dg₁ = dg₂:
v₁ dp − s₁ dT = v₂ dp − s₂ dT
blocks.where: v₁, s₁ are for phase 1 at the point; v₂, s₂ are for phase 2.

blocks.text: This is the Clapeyron equation. It assumes no ideal gas and holds for any phase pair: solid-liquid, liquid-vapour, solid-vapour, even two solid forms. Some syllabi call it the Clapeyron equation and reserve Clausius-Clapeyron for the vapour form.

sections.h3: The vapour form: ideal gas, small liquid volume

blocks.text: Apply it to liquid and vapour. Take phase 1 as vapour, phase 2 as liquid:
dp/dT = h_fg/(T v_fg), with v_fg = v_g − v_f
blocks.where: h_fg is latent heat of vaporisation (kJ/kg); v_g and v_f are specific volumes of saturated vapour and liquid (m³/kg).

blocks.text: Two approximations make it usable from vapour-pressure data. Far below the critical point v_f ≪ v_g, so v_fg ≈ v_g. Treat the vapour as ideal gas: v_g = RT/p, with R the vapour gas constant (kJ/kg·K). Substituting:
d(ln p)/dT = h_fg/(R T²),  or  d(ln p)/d(1/T) = −h_fg/R
blocks.where: ln p is natural log of saturation pressure; the slope of ln p against 1/T is −h_fg/R, in kelvin.

blocks.text: This is the Clausius-Clapeyron equation. A plot of ln p against 1/T is nearly straight over a short range, with slope −h_fg/R. That slope gives average h_fg. With h_fg constant, integrate between two states:

blocks.where: p₁, T₁ are a known saturation pair; p₂, T₂ the unknown pair; both T in kelvin. h_fg/R has units K, so the right side is a plain number.

sections.h3: Reading the sign: melting lines and boiling lines

blocks.text: For melting, the same equation gives dp/dT = h_fus/(T v_fus), where h_fus is latent heat of fusion and v_fus = v_liquid − v_solid. Most solids are denser than their liquids, so v_fus is positive and the melting line leans forward: pressure raises the melting point.

Water reverses this because ice is less dense than liquid water. v_fus is negative, so dp/dT is negative, about −1.3 × 10⁷ Pa/K; dT/dp ≈ −0.0074 K per atmosphere. The melting point of ice falls as pressure rises. This is regelation: a weighted wire melts ice below it, water flows up and refreezes above, and the block ends whole. Pressure melting is only one contributor to skating; friction and the liquid-like surface layer do most of the work.

On the liquid-vapour line dp/dT is always positive and grows with T, so the curve bends upward and steepens. A pressure cooker at about 2 bar boils water hotter and cooks faster; boiling point falls with altitude. Run backwards, the curve gives h_fg from two pressure readings, or saturation pressure at an unmeasured temperature.

figure.caption: Saturation pressure of water against temperature from the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation. The marked input is 101.3 kPa at 373 K; the model estimate for 323 K is 13.3 kPa, against a steam-table value of about 12.3 kPa. The curve flattens at the low-temperature end and steepens as T rises.

spec.aria: The saturation curve rises steeply with temperature. The plotted input is 101.3 kPa at 373 K; the model estimate at 323 K is 13.3 kPa, while the true value is about 12.3 kPa.

examples.question: Water boils at T₁ = 373 K where p₁ = 101.3 kPa. Take h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg and R = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K for steam. Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation with h_fg held constant, estimate the saturation pressure at T₂ = 323 K, and say why the answer differs from the steam-table value of about 12.3 kPa.
steps: Both temperatures are already in kelvin.

Comment: the estimate is about 8 per cent high. The real h_fg rises from 2257 to about 2382 kJ/kg between 373 K and 323 K, and the vapour is not perfectly ideal; both approximations matter more over a wide gap.
examples.answer: The estimated saturation pressure at 323 K is 13.3 kPa, against about 12.3 kPa from the steam tables.
examples.check:
import math
hfg = 2257.0
R = 0.4615
T1, T2 = 373.0, 323.0
p1 = 101.3
d = 1/T2 - 1/T1
ratio = hfg/R
lnp = -ratio*d
p2 = p1*math.exp(lnp)
print(round(ratio, 2))
print(round(d, 8))
print(round(lnp, 4))
print(round(p2, 2))

traps: Using Celsius in ln p or the exponent. The integrated form needs kelvin; 50 instead of 323 is nonsense.
Mixing units so h_fg and R are not both per kg. 2257 kJ/kg with 461.5 J/kg·K makes h_fg/R a thousand times too small.
Using v_fg ≈ v_g and ideal vapour near the critical point, where v_f and v_g are both large and nearly equal. Use full Clapeyron with table values there.
Assuming every melting line slopes forward. Ice is the standard exception: v_fus is negative, so dp/dT is negative.
Stretching the integrated form over a wide band while claiming h_fg constant. Say the estimate is approximate.

quiz.q: State the Clapeyron equation and define every symbol with its unit.
quiz.a: dp/dT = h₁₂/(T v₁₂). dp/dT is saturation-line slope (Pa/K); h₁₂ is latent heat (J/kg); T is absolute temperature (K); v₁₂ is specific-volume change (m³/kg).

quiz.q: For ln p plotted against 1/T, what is the slope and what does it give?
quiz.a: Slope is −h_fg/R, in kelvin. Multiply its magnitude by R to get h_fg.

quiz.q: Why is s₁ − s₂ equal to h₁₂/T for a phase change?
quiz.a: A phase change at fixed pressure happens at constant T. The reversible heat per kg is h₁₂, so entropy change is ∫dQ/T = h₁₂/T.

quiz.q: Why does the ice-water melting line slope backwards while most substances' melting lines slope forward?
quiz.a: Slope is h_fus/(T v_fus), v_fus = v_liquid − v_solid. Most solids are denser, so v_fus > 0 and slope > 0. Ice is less dense than water, so v_fus < 0 and slope < 0: pressure lowers the melting point.

quiz.q: Using p₁ = 101.3 kPa at T₁ = 373 K, h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg and R = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K, estimate the saturation pressure at 353 K.
A plot of ln p against 1/T has slope −4891 K. Find h_fg if R = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K.
The Clausius-Clapeyron estimate at 323 K came out above the steam-table value. Which assumption is mainly responsible, and in which direction does it push the answer?
quiz.a: Constant h_fg mainly. Real h_fg at 323 K is about 2382 kJ/kg, larger than 2257, so true exponent is more negative and true pressure lower. Ideal-gas error is smaller. Hence the estimate overshoots: 13.3 kPa against 12.3 kPa.

quiz.q: At the critical point both h_fg and v_fg tend to zero. What does the Clapeyron equation say about dp/dT there?
quiz.a: h_fg/(T v_fg) keeps a finite limit as both tend to zero, so the curve ends at the critical point with finite slope; it does not become infinite. The limiting ratio gives the value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real vapour-pressure curves use the Antoine equation, log₁₀ p = A − B/(C + T), with three constants and a wide accurate range; the Wagner equation does better near the critical point. Chemical engineers use these fits to size distillation columns, where two components' vapour pressures decide separation. Atmospheric science uses the curve for humidity, and freeze-drying sets ice temperature for sublimation. Search next for the Antoine equation, Wagner equation, and Knudsen effusion method for latent heats.
